title: The May 1904 Lunch in Manchester Where Rolls First Met Royce
dek: A friend brought a London car dealer north to meet a Manchester electrical engineer, and a small two-cylinder car settled the matter.

story.event: The first meeting of Rolls and Royce in Manchester and Rolls's decision to sell all of Royce's cars
story.summary: On 4 May 1904 Henry Edmunds introduced the London car dealer Charles Rolls to the Manchester electrical engineer Henry Royce, who had built three small two-cylinder cars; after driving one, Rolls agreed to sell as many as Royce could make under the name Rolls-Royce. The arrangement was put in writing on 23 December 1904 and Rolls-Royce Limited was registered in March 1906. Tradition places the lunch at the Midland Hotel, though Edmunds remembered a 'Great Central Hotel'.
paragraphs: On Wednesday 4 May 1904, Charles Rolls, a 26-year-old London car dealer and racing motorist, had lunch in Manchester with Henry Royce, an engineer fourteen years older who had been earning his keep since the age of nine. The introduction was made by Henry Edmunds, a friend of Rolls from the motoring world and a shareholder in Royce's firm. Manchester places the lunch at the Midland Hotel, but Edmunds remembered a "Great Central Hotel", and no hotel of that name appears in the city's 1904 directory.

Each man had something the other lacked. Rolls and his partner, Claude Johnson, sold cars imported from France and Belgium, and Rolls wanted a British car good enough to carry his own name. Royce had run an electrical business in Manchester since 1884, making fittings, dynamos and cranes, but in the early 1900s a downturn and cheaper foreign motors were squeezing it. Unimpressed by a second-hand French Decauville, he designed his own car and built three small two-cylinder Royces, the first on the road in April 1904. Edmunds drove one in a trial that spring and was impressed. By Richard Cavendish's account in History Today, Edmunds all but dragged Rolls to Manchester.

Edmunds recalled that the two men took to each other at first sight. Rolls drove the little car, and the company's own history says he agreed there and then to sell as many cars as Royce could make, under both their names. Cavendish has him borrowing it, driving it to London and waking Johnson in the night for a ride. The company says Rolls told Johnson he had found "the greatest motor engineer in the world." Rolls later described Royce as a man of "exceptional ingenuity and power of overcoming difficulties."

The handshake still had to be written down. On 23 December 1904, Rolls and Johnson, trading as C. S. Rolls & Co., agreed to market the whole output of Royce's car works, a range running from a two-cylinder 10 hp to a six-cylinder 30 hp, sold as Rolls-Royce. In March 1906 the venture was registered as Rolls-Royce Limited. Rolls saw little of it: he was killed at a Bournemouth air show in 1910, aged 32. Royce, often ill, kept checking and drawing designs until he died in 1933.

quote.text: As the first thing man requires of man is reality, so that appears in all the forms of society. We pointedly, and by name, introduce the parties to each other.
quote.source_title: Essays — Second Series, Project Gutenberg eBook #2945
quote.connection: Rolls had heard Edmunds praise Royce's car before he went north; what settled it was sitting across a table from the man and driving the car himself. Emerson says the first thing we ask of one another is reality, and that the old ritual of introduction, names spoken face to face, exists to supply it.

reflection: Rolls knew about Royce's car before he went. What changed things was sitting opposite the man who made it and taking it out on the road himself. Some judgements cannot be made from a distance, however good the report, and finding out often costs no more than a train ticket and a lunch.

The person easiest to overlook in this story is Edmunds. His name is not on the badge. He saw that two people who needed each other had never met, and he took the trouble to fix it. You probably know two such people. An introduction costs you a few lines, and it can matter more to them than anything else you do this week.
invitation: Think of two people you know who would be useful to each other and have never met. Write the two or three sentences that would introduce them, and send it today if it still feels right.

research_notes: Venue: the Rolls-Royce company, the BBC (2004 centenary) and the Midland Hotel's plaques place the lunch at the Midland Hotel. Edmunds's own reminiscence, as reported by I Love Manchester from Ed Glinert's research, names the 'Great Central Hotel'; History Today (2004) writes 'Grand Central Hotel'; Motor Sport (1979) asserts the Midland was then called the Great Central, while Glinert notes that Kelly's 1904 directory lists no Great Central Hotel and argues for refreshment rooms near London Road station. The story gives the tradition and Edmunds's wording side by side and does not settle it. Rolls's remark to Johnson: the company newsroom gives 'the greatest motor engineer in the world'; a quoted excerpt from the book Rolls-Royce: The Magic of a Name gives 'the greatest engineer in the world'; the story quotes the company's wording and attributes it to the company. Introduction wording also varies between the two company newsroom pages ('Henry, may I introduce Charles Rolls' and '...The Honourable Charles Rolls'), so it is not quoted. Rolls's imports: Rolls-Royce Motor Cars says Peugeot and Minerva; Grace's Guide says Panhard, Orleans and Minerva; the story says only French and Belgian. Royce's first car: the company says April 1904; Grace's Guide's timeline line '1904 December The first Royce car was made' conflicts with every other source and with Edmunds driving one in April, so it is not used. How Edmunds had the car: the company says he borrowed Royce's first 10 hp for the Side Slip Trials at the end of April 1904; CarsGuide and the Calderdale Companion say Royce sold him one; the story says only that he drove one. Rolls 'agreed on the spot' (company) while the written agreement with C. S. Rolls & Co. is dated 23 December 1904 (Grace's Guide); the story gives both as a handshake followed by a contract. Motor Sport says Rolls and Edmunds travelled up the day before; other accounts imply the same day; the story does not say. The claim that Edmunds 'more or less dragged' Rolls north rests on History Today alone and is attributed to Cavendish. Funding is 'mixed': the cars were built with the resources of Royce's established, publicly floated electrical company and sold through Rolls's dealership, and the 1906 company was capitalised at £60,000 by a share issue.
